chunks.text: unit i: foundations of nlp natural language processing (nlp) what is it? nlp is the branch of ai concerned with giving computers the ability to understand, interpret, and generate human language in a valuable way. the core problem: humans communicate in messy, context-dependent ways. computers only understand rigid mathematics. nlp is the translator between these two worlds. applications of nlp •machine translation (google translate) •chatbots and virtual assistants (chatgpt, siri, alexa) •sentiment analysis •spam email detection •text summarization •question answering systems phase time period main approach example rule-based era 1950s–late 1980s handcrafted grammar and dictionary rules rule-based machine translation statistical nlp era 1990s–early 2010s probability and machine learning spam detection, statistical mt deep learning era <num> –present neural networks and transformers chatgpt, google translate, bert, gpt language and grammar (machines vs humans) <num> aspect humans machines (nlp systems) understanding understand meaning using context, experience, and common sense. understand text using rules, algorithms, and learned patterns from data. grammar can recognize correct grammar even with incomplete or informal sentences. depend on grammar rules or trained models; may struggle with ambiguous or incorrect sentences. context easily infer hidden meanings, emotions, sarcasm, and intent. need contextual data and models; sarcasm and implicit meaning are more difficult. learning learn naturally through interaction and experience. learn from large datasets using machine learning or deep learning. error handling can understand and correct grammatical mistakes intuitively. may misinterpret sentences if grammar is incorrect or unseen during training. flexibility adapt quickly to new words, slang, and language changes. require retraining or fine-tuning to handle new language patterns effectively. concept example <num> . language as structured communication sentence: "the cat sat on the mat." grammar and syntax help identify that "cat" is the subject, "sat" is the verb, and "on the mat" indicates location. this allows the system to understand the sentence correctly. <num> . knowledge represents meaning

chunks.text: "cat" is the subject, "sat" is the verb, and "on the mat" indicates location. this allows the system to understand the sentence correctly. <num> . knowledge represents meaning sentence: "apple released a new iphone." knowledge helps identify that apple refers to the technology company, not the fruit, based on context. <num> . symbolic approaches used explicit knowledge a rule-based grammar checker may use the rule: "a singular subject must take a singular verb." it flags the sentence "she go to school." and corrects it to "she goes to school." <num> . statistical and neural models learn implicit knowledge a transformer model like gpt learns from millions of sentences that after "the capital of france is...", the most likely next word is "paris", without being explicitly programmed with this rule. <num> . integration of language and knowledge boosts understanding question: "who wrote harry potter?" a language model combined with external knowledge can accurately answer "j.k. rowling" and even provide related information such as the publication year or book series. where morphology is used (real applications) <num> common stemming algorithms • porter stemmer: standard and widely used rule-based stemmer with good accuracy. • snowball stemmer: improved version of porter; chunks.text: in nlp? a. to increase sentence length b. to convert text into numerical form c. to improve grammar d. to translate text correct answer: b machine learning models work with numbers, so text must be converted into numerical form. quiz which of the following is true about bag of words (bow)? a. it preserves word order b. it understands grammar c. it counts word frequency d. it captures word meaning correct answer: c bow represents text using word counts and ignores grammar and order. what is an n-gram? a. a random group of words b. a sequence of n consecutive words or characters c. a type of neural network d. a stop-word list correct answer: b an n-gram is a continuous sequence of n items from text. which of the following is an advantage of n- grams over bag of words? a. requires less memory b. ignores word order c. captures context and word order d. reduces vocabulary size correct answer: c n-grams preserve word sequence, which helps capture context. what is an out-of-vocabulary (oov) word? a. a frequently used word b. a word removed during preprocessing c. a word not present in training data d. a stop-word correct answer: c oov words are unseen words that were not present in the training vocabulary. why is punctuation removal done in nlp? a. to improve grammar b. to reduce noise and simplify text c. to increase accuracy of spelling d. to increase sentence length correct answer: b punctuation usually does not contribute to meaning and increases data complexity. nlp preprocessing pipeline (google colab) ✔covers: ✔tokenization ✔lowercasing ✔noise removal ✔stopword removal ✔stemming & lemmatization ✔bag-of-words ✔tf–idf ✔uses tensorflow / keras compatible tools lab1: given a set of text documents, implement a preprocessing pipeline that performs: tokenization lowercasing noise removal stopword removal stemming/lemmatization converts the processed text into numerical representations using

chunks.text: ✔uses tensorflow / keras compatible tools lab1: given a set of text documents, implement a preprocessing pipeline that performs: tokenization lowercasing noise removal stopword removal stemming/lemmatization converts the processed text into numerical representations using bag-of-words and tf-idf install & import libraries # install required libraries (run once in colab) !pip install nltk scikit-learn import re import nltk import string from nltk.corpus import stopwords from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize from nltk.stem import porterstemmer, wordnetlemmatizer from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import countvectorizer, tfidfvectorizer •pip is python's package manager •nltk → natural language toolkit (classical nlp tasks) •scikit-learn → converts text into numerical features •colab does not come with all libraries → we install them manually •re → regular expressions (pattern-based text cleaning) •nltk → tokenization, stopwords, stemming, lemmatization •string → contains predefined punctuation symbols •stopwords → common words like is, the, and •word_tokenize → splits sentence into words •porterstemmer → reduces words to root form •wordnetlemmatizer → converts words to dictionary form •countvectorizer → bag-of-words •tfidfvectorizer → tf-idf representation download nltk resources nltk.download('punkt') nltk.download('stopwords') nltk.download('wordnet') nltk.download('omw- <num> ') explaination: •nltk does not ship data by default •punkt → tokenizer model •stopwords → stopword list •wordnet → lexical database for lemmatization •omw → improves lemmatizer accuracy input text documents documents = [ "natural language processing is a fascinating field of ai!", "text preprocessing includes tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization.", "machine learning models require numerical input, not raw text." ] explaination: •this is a corpus (collection of documents) •each sentence is treated as one document •real datasets come from files, csvs, or databases initialize nlp tools stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english')) •loads english stopwords
chunks.label: hard

chunks.text: •each sentence is treated as one document •real datasets come from files, csvs, or databases initialize nlp tools stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english')) •loads english stopwords •converted to set → faster lookup than list stemmer = porterstemmer() •creates a stemming object •example: running → run lemmatizer = wordnetlemmatizer() •creates lemmatizer object •example: better → good define preprocessing function def preprocess_text(text): •function processes one document at a time •reusable for entire corpus lowercasing text = text.lower() •converts all text to lowercase •avoids treating ai and ai as different words noise removal text = re.sub(r'\d+', '', text) •removes numbers •\d+ → one or more digits text = text.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation)) •removes punctuation symbols like .,!? •keeps only meaningful text tokenization tokens = word_tokenize(text) •splits sentence into words •example: "nlp is fun" → ['nlp', 'is', 'fun'] stopword removal tokens = [word for word in tokens if word not in stop_words] •removes words that add little meaning •reduces dimensionality •improves model focus stemming stemmed_tokens = [stemmer.stem(word) for word in tokens] •cuts words to root form •fast but not linguistically perfect lemmatization lemmatized_tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(word) for word in stemmed_tokens] •converts word to valid dictionary word •more meaningful than stemming •slower but accurate join tokens back return ' '.join(lemmatized_tokens) •converts list of words back into sentence •required by countvectorizer and tfidfvectorizer apply preprocessing to all documents processed_documents = [preprocess_text(doc) for doc in documents] •applies preprocessing function to every document •output → clean corpus for i, doc in enumerate(processed_documents): print(f"processed document {i+ <num> }: {doc}") •displays cleaned text
chunks.label: hard

chunks.text: •output → clean corpus for i, doc in enumerate(processed_documents): print(f"processed document {i+ <num> }: {doc}") •displays cleaned text •useful for debugging and teaching bag-of-words (bow) bow_vectorizer = countvectorizer() •initializes bow model bow_features = bow_vectorizer.fit_transform(processed_documents) •fit → builds vocabulary •transform → converts text into vectors bow_vectorizer.get_feature_names_out() •displays vocabulary (columns) bow_features.toarray() •rows → documents •columns → word frequency tf-idf representation tfidf_vectorizer = tfidfvectorizer() •initializes tf-idf model tfidf_features = tfidf_vectorizer.fit_transform(processed_documents) •weighs words by importance, not just frequency tfidf_features.toarray() •values between <num> and <num> •rare but important words get higher weight quiz what is the effect of the line text = re.sub(r'\d+', '', text) in the preprocessing pipeline? a. removes all punctuation symbols b. replaces digits with whitespace c. removes all numeric characters from the text d. converts digits into words correct answer: c the regex \d+ matches one or more digits and removes them completely. quiz which of the following best explains why stopwords are stored as a set? stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english')) a. sets preserve word order b. sets allow duplicate stopwords c. sets provide faster membership checking d. sets reduce memory usage automatically correct answer: c checking word in stop_words is faster in a set than in a list. quiz in the code, stemming is applied before lemmatization: stemmed_tokens = [stemmer.stem(word) for word in tokens] lemmatized_tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(word) for word in stemmed_tokens] what is the main drawback of this order? a. it increases computational cost b. lemmatization may receive non-dictionary words c. stemming becomes linguistically accurate d. stopword removal becomes ineffective correct answer: b explanation: stemming can produce invalid roots, reducing lemmatization effectiveness. quiz
chunks.label: medium

chunks.text: b. lemmatization may receive non-dictionary words c. stemming becomes linguistically accurate d. stopword removal becomes ineffective correct answer: b explanation: stemming can produce invalid roots, reducing lemmatization effectiveness. quiz what does each row in the bag-of-words matrix represent? bow_features.toarray() a. a unique word in the corpus b. a document represented as word frequencies c. a stopword vector d. a tf-idf weight vector correct answer: b rows correspond to documents; columns correspond to vocabulary terms. quiz why does tf-idf assign lower weight to commonly occurring words? a. because such words are removed as stopwords b. because tf-idf ignores word frequency c. because frequent words have low discriminative power d. because tf-idf uses binary features correct answer: c tf-idf penalizes common words since they contribute less to distinguishing documents. quiz in the preprocessing function, why is the line text = text.lower() applied before tokenization? a. to reduce the size of the stopword list b. to ensure that words like “ai” and “ai” are treated as the same token c. to improve stemming accuracy only d. to remove punctuation automatically correct answer: b lowercasing avoids duplicate tokens caused by case differences, reducing vocabulary size. references <num> . l <num> nlp basics( tokenization, stemming, lemmatization, stopwords) <num> . natural language processing (prof. pawan goyal, iit kharagpur): lecture <num> - pcfgs - inside-outside probabilities <num> . text analytics concepts: tf-idf, bag-of-words explained with examples
